what contradicts: Copilot field experiment — the abstract describes a controlled experiment in which recruited developers were given a set task, not a field experiment

close the gap with real images for classification — the abstract says the clones close only "a large part of the gap", not the whole gap | "ImageNet clones trained from class names alone" — the abstract says the clones are generated from class names; it is the classification models that are trained, on the clones

enabling 2.8× faster model training — the abstract says subject matter experts build models 2.8× faster in a user study (human development speed, not training speed); the speedup tied to execution is up to 1.8× per pipeline execution from the optimizer
matches ELMo — the abstract says only "comparable results with ELMo", a slightly weaker claim

matches ELMo performance — the abstract says only "comparable results with ELMo" | "100× fewer parameters and 15× faster inference" — the abstract says "roughly 100 times" and "15 times less inference time"; the summary drops the approximation

achieving +34% sensitivity improvement: the abstract says "up to +34%" of sensitivity rate improvement, i.e. a maximum, and only for the transformation combined with the best known regression adjustment; the summary states it as the flat result of the transformation.

improve single-image super-resolution over per-pixel losses is slightly stronger than the abstract, which only says replacing a per-pixel loss with a perceptual loss 'gives visually pleasing results', not a general improvement | "at three orders of magnitude lower cost": the abstract says the network is 'three orders of magnitude faster' (speed), not lower cost; a loose rewording rather than a hard contradiction

factorizing model computations into interpretable input-dependent and input-invariant terms: the abstract says the resulting circuits factorize into input-dependent and input-invariant terms; it does not say model computations are factorized or that the terms themselves are interpretable (it says computations are decomposed into interpretable circuits).
finding frontier horizons of about 50 minutes — the abstract says frontier models such as o3 have a 50% time horizon of around 110 minutes; the 50 is the success rate, not the horizon length
standard alignment reduces distributional pluralism states this as an established result; the abstract only says standard alignment procedures "might reduce distributional pluralism"
in a second: the abstract says "in less than a second" (minor imprecision, echoes the title)
with 230× speedup: the abstract says "up to 230× speedup", an upper bound rather than a flat figure

they improve click prediction but not ranking quality against expert relevance labels — the abstract says ULTR techniques "struggle to consistently improve ranking performance" and that click gains "do not necessarily translate" into ranking gains; it reports inconsistent improvement, not a flat absence of improvement.
